case_study_insert.main_stem: Harborview Hotel Group (HHG) is a private limited company in the hospitality and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2001 by Elena Vasquez, it runs a chain of coastal boutique hotels and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. HHG plans to invest $900,000 in refurbishing its flagship property with energy-efficient systems, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,200,000 a year, a variable cost of $60 per room-night and a selling price of $180 per room-night, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. HHG faces two problems: guest complaints about room cleanliness are rising and annual staff turnover has reached 18%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Guest Experience and Operations Report, Q4 2025: HHG recorded 9,800 room-nights in the quarter at an average occupancy of 71%, down from 78% a year earlier. Room-cleanliness complaints rose from 26 to 47 per month and the quality team logged 38 replaced linen sets. Average check-in wait was 11 minutes against a 5-minute target. A survey of 500 guests found 68% would pay $15 more for an energy-efficient refurbished room, while 55% choose their hotel on cleanliness reviews. Cleaning staff retraining at the local college costs $450 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harborview Hotel Group as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for hotels with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.40 to $13.08 per hour from April 2026, lifting housekeeping wage bills. (3) Hotel energy and linen input costs have risen 9.2% year-on-year, while domestic tourism spending grew 4.1% and inflation is 6.3%.

questions.question_text: HHG plans to finance part of its $900,000 refurbishment with retained profit. Explain two advantages for HHG of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $300,000 requires no interest payments or capital repayment, so HHG avoids adding to the interest burden created by its $600,000 ten-year bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen to 5.0%. The cash saved can help absorb the 9.2% rise in energy and linen costs and protect the $120 contribution per room-night without raising the $180 selling price, which matters because surveyed guests are already sensitive to price and cleanliness. Every dollar of interest avoided improves the operating profit available to tackle the 18% staff-turnover problem.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps control with the existing owners, since no lender can impose conditions on how the flagship hotel is refurbished or how the 60-strong workforce is organised. It also avoids the repossession risk that would put HHG's $3,800,000 of non-current assets at stake if refurbished rooms failed to lift the 71% occupancy rate. Because the money is already inside the business, the energy-efficient refurbishment can start immediately rather than waiting for loan approval.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to HHG's refurbishment, costs and financing.

questions.question_text: HHG is choosing how to promote its refurbished flagship hotel. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HHG choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build awareness of the refurbished rooms across the country and could attract inbound tourists, which matters as tourism spending grows. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a business carrying a $600,000 bank loan and $1,200,000 fixed costs, and most viewers will never book a coastal boutique hotel, so much of the spend is wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is far cheaper and reaches the domestic market that makes up much of HHG's 71% occupancy, and it can carry a time-limited refurbishment message. Its weakness is narrow reach: it cannot reach the 68% of 500 surveyed guests who would pay $15 more if they live outside the broadcast area, so it cannot fill 40,000 room-nights by itself.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can show the energy-efficient refurbished rooms directly to the 68% of surveyed guests willing to pay $15 more and the 55% who choose on cleanliness reviews. It is measurable, much cheaper than television, and its reach is national, though results build slowly and depend on influencer credibility.

Recommendation: HHG should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets precisely the segment the survey identified, costs far less than television, and reaches beyond radio's local catchment while reinforcing the cleanliness message needed to cut the 47 monthly complaints. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted given the $900,000 refurbishment and loan commitments; radio is rejected as too narrow to lift occupancy back toward the 78% level of a year earlier.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HHG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in HHG's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in HHG's context with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: HHG's cleanliness complaints have risen to 47 per month and staff turnover is 18%. Explain two benefits for HHG of introducing team working among its housekeeping staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets housekeeping staff share a common cleaning checklist for the refurbished rooms, so the 47 monthly complaints can be tackled collectively rather than by isolated individuals. Under a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, formal teams give staff a route to report pinch points and standardise room preparation, improving the guest experience that drives the 55% of surveyed guests who choose a hotel on cleanliness reviews. Teams also spread the workload when occupancy is high, so the 71% occupancy rate does not lead to rushed cleaning.

Point 2: Working in teams raises job satisfaction and a sense of belonging, which should reduce the 18% staff turnover that currently forces repeated $450-per-employee retraining. Experienced room attendants can coach new recruits on the new energy-efficient systems, cutting the induction burden on the 60-strong workforce and protecting the 40,000 room-nights target while the flagship property is being refurbished. Because the $900,000 refurbishment changes room layouts, teams can share the updated checklist quickly, cutting the time new recruits take to reach the required standard.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to HHG's complaints, turnover and workforce.

questions.question_text: HHG must reduce its 18% housekeeping staff turnover. Consider paying a financial bonus or introducing job enrichment. Which should HHG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Financial bonus: A cash bonus tied to cleanliness scores would directly reward staff for cutting the 47 monthly complaints, and because it is a variable payment it need not permanently raise the $1,200,000 fixed costs. It is easy to understand and can be paid only when occupancy and guest-review targets are met. However, with a $600,000 bank loan and a $900,000 refurbishment, cash is tight, and a bonus across all 60 staff would swell the wage bill exactly as the 5.5% minimum-wage rise takes effect. Bonuses can also narrow focus to measured tasks only.

Job enrichment: Giving housekeepers responsibility for their own floor, a say in cleanliness standards and rotation onto the new energy-efficient systems addresses the root cause of the 18% turnover by making the work more meaningful. It fits the refurbished flagship and reduces the $450-per-employee retraining cost because staff stay longer. It uses little cash, but it consumes management time, may be resisted in a hierarchical/autocratic culture, and works gradually.

Decision: HHG should choose job enrichment, adding a small bonus only after complaints fall. Job enrichment tackles the 18% turnover directly, costs little while loan repayments and the refurbishment absorb cash, and suits a 60-strong workforce. A large universal bonus is rejected because it raises costs during a 5.5% wage rise and treats symptoms only, whereas the 47 complaints need genuine ownership. A bonus would also need a fair cleanliness measure, which the current 47 complaints show is inconsistent. Managers should review complaints monthly so the choice can be judged against the 47-card baseline.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two methods with limited application to HHG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in HHG's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in context with a justified decision covering cost, culture and staff turnover.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HHG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,200,000 ÷ ($180 − $60) = $1,200,000 ÷ $120 = 10,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 10,000 room-nights a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $180 − $60 = $120. Answer: contribution per unit is $120.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HHG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HHG can compare the 10,000-room-night break-even with actual output of 40,000 room-nights, giving a margin of safety of 30,000 room-nights, so managers can judge how far occupancy can fall from 71% before losses begin during the refurbishment.
2. The $120 contribution lets managers test the survey premium: if all rooms achieved the $15 extra, contribution would be $135 and break-even $1,200,000 ÷ $135 = 8,889 room-nights, showing the refurbishment's potential.
3. Managers can use break-even to set the occupancy target needed to service the $600,000 loan, checking that 40,000 room-nights cover the $1,200,000 fixed costs plus interest.
4. Average total cost of $1,200,000 ÷ 40,000 + $60 = $90 per room-night can be benchmarked each quarter to spot the 9.2% energy-cost rise early and judge whether the $450 retraining spend is worthwhile.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 10,000 room-nights | (ii) Contribution per unit = $120 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 40,000 room-nights; $15 premium and revised break-even of 8,889; loan-service volume target; and average total cost of $90 to track the 9.2% energy rise.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HHG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HHG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.53 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.93 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $220,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $460,000; 2025 current assets = $150,000 + $260,000 + $90,000 = $500,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $460,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.53; 2025 = $500,000 ÷ $290,000 = 1.72. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($460,000 − $180,000) ÷ $300,000 = $280,000 ÷ $300,000 = 0.93; 2025 = ($500,000 − $150,000) ÷ $290,000 = $350,000 ÷ $290,000 = 1.21.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. Trade receivables rose from $220,000 to $260,000 and cash from $60,000 to $90,000, so more of the $500,000 current assets are near-cash, while current liabilities fell to $290,000. The stricter test, which removes inventories, also improved from 0.93 to 1.21, so HHG is less dependent on selling stock to pay near-term bills — important while it services a $600,000 loan and spends $900,000 on refurbishment. However, rising receivables tie up cash; if hotel clients pay late, the improvement could reverse, and inventories of $150,000 still need managing. The $3,800,000 of non-current assets makes the balance sheet asset-heavy, so short-term liquidity deserves close attention while the flagship is out of action.

Conclusion: HHG's financial position has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement does not rely on inventory. The main residual risk is higher trade receivables, so tighter credit control is advisable before further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on HHG's financial position.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HHG of introducing the energy-efficient refurbishment at its flagship hotel.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Energy-efficient systems directly attack the 9.2% rise in energy and linen input costs, lowering the $60 variable cost per room-night and protecting the $120 contribution without raising the $180 price. The survey found 68% of 500 guests would pay $15 more for such a refurbished room, so HHG could earn a premium that helps justify the $900,000 investment and improves the 71% occupancy rate, helping recovery toward the 78% level of a year earlier.

Disadvantage: The $900,000 outlay adds to a $600,000 bank loan when the base rate has reached 5.0%, raising financing risk if refurbished rooms do not attract the expected demand. Works may also disrupt the 40,000 room-nights target, and if cleanliness complaints (already 47 a month) are not solved, the premium may not be realised, delaying payback. If 18% turnover continues, staff may not sustain the higher standard, wasting the investment. Careful cost tracking each quarter will show whether the $15 premium is actually being achieved.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HHG's costs, survey data and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.2% rise in energy and linen input costs will affect HHG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If HHG's $600,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point increase adds 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year, which is small beside $1,200,000 fixed costs; if the loan is fixed, the direct effect is zero. Higher rates may also make the $900,000 refurbishment dearer to finance and deter discretionary guests, but the risk can be capped by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.08 per hour): With a workforce of 60 in housekeeping and front-of-house, this lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 40,000 room-nights ÷ 60 staff = about 667 room-nights per employee. If productivity holds or refurbished rooms lift 71% occupancy, the extra cost per room-night is small; if not, the $120 contribution is squeezed.

Energy and linen input costs (+9.2%): These feed the $60 variable cost per room-night. As an illustrative upper bound, if the whole $60 rose 9.2% that is $5.52 per room-night (9.2% × $60), or about $220,800 a year at 40,000 room-nights. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution below $120, and the $15 premium accepted by 68% of surveyed guests offsets only part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.2% input-cost rise has the greatest impact: it applies to every one of the 40,000 room-nights, directly erodes the $120 contribution that justifies the $900,000 investment, and recurs annually, unlike the capped, one-off interest effect and the productivity-dependent wage effect.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HHG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HHG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in HHG's context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
